oneSentence: An AI system built for a limited task or related tasks, rather than broad intellectual work across domains.
plainExplanation:
Narrow AI means an AI system designed for a particular kind of job. That job might be translating text, spotting objects in images, recommending songs, or choosing the next word in a sentence. It can produce useful results in that area, but that does not mean it can handle unrelated tasks reliably.

What goes in depends on the system. Inputs might be text, images, sound, numbers, or clicks from users. The system then applies rules or a trained model. A model is a mathematical system adjusted from examples so it can produce outputs for new inputs. The output could be a label, a score, a prediction, or generated text.

Many current AI tools are narrow AI, even when they seem broad at first glance. A chatbot may answer questions, summarise, translate, and draft messages, but it still works within the kinds of patterns it was built and trained for. If the task changes too much, the system may fail, guess, or produce convincing but wrong output.

People often confuse narrow AI with human-like intelligence. They are not the same. Narrow AI can be very strong at one task and still lack the flexible, general capability people usually imagine in science fiction. The boundary is not perfectly agreed, especially for newer systems that can do many related tasks, so the term is useful but not always precise.

everydayAnalogy.title: The airport desk with one job
everydayAnalogy.story: At an airport, one desk only checks boarding passes and passports. The staff there can do that task quickly and accurately for thousands of travellers. But if a traveller asks about lost baggage, visa policy, or how to repair a broken phone charger, that desk cannot handle it and sends them elsewhere. It works well for its assigned task, not for every problem in the airport.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A desk worker is a person with broad real-world abilities, even if their role is narrow. Narrow AI does not secretly have general ability behind the scenes. Also, many AI systems do not follow one simple checklist like the desk does; some use learned statistical patterns from large datasets, which makes their behaviour less transparent than a desk procedure.

visual.title: Narrow AI: strong in one lane, limited outside it
visual.learningObjective: Show why a system can perform well on a defined task without having broad, human-like capability across unrelated tasks.
visual.description: A two-column comparison. The left column shows one AI system receiving inputs that match its designed task and producing useful outputs. The right column shows the same system receiving unrelated inputs and producing poor, uncertain, or no results. Read top to bottom in each column, then compare the outcomes.

steps.label: Designed task
steps.explanation: The system is built or trained for a specific job, such as translating short text or choosing the next word in a sentence.
steps.visualInstruction: Top row spanning both columns: a box labelled 'One narrow AI system'. Under it, add a note: 'Built for a defined task or related task family'.

steps.label: Input fits the task
steps.explanation: When the input matches that job, the system can often perform well.
steps.visualInstruction: Left column middle: arrows from icons for text, image, or numbers into the system box. Label them 'expected inputs'.

steps.label: Useful output
steps.explanation: The result may be a prediction, label, ranking, or generated text.
steps.visualInstruction: Left column bottom: arrows out to boxes labelled 'translation', 'spam score', 'next word', or 'detected object'. Use a green accent.

steps.label: Input does not fit
steps.explanation: When asked to do something outside its design or training, performance can drop sharply.
steps.visualInstruction: Right column middle: arrows from mismatched icons into the same system box. Label them 'unrelated or out-of-scope inputs'.

steps.label: Weak or unreliable result
steps.explanation: The system may fail, guess, or produce a confident-looking but unsuitable answer.
steps.visualInstruction: Right column bottom: arrows out to boxes labelled 'error', 'poor guess', or 'unreliable output'. Use an amber or red accent.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each bottom output box to reveal a short note explaining why it is in-scope or out-of-scope for the same system.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This comparison diagram explains narrow AI by showing one system in two situations. At the top is a box labelled 'One narrow AI system', with a note that it was built for a defined task or a family of related tasks. In the left column, expected inputs such as text, images, or numbers go into the system. The outputs are useful results, such as a translation, a spam score, a next-word suggestion, or an object label. In the right column, unrelated or out-of-scope inputs go into the same system. The outputs are marked as error, poor guess, or unreliable output. The main point is that the same system can work well inside its intended scope and fail outside it.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static side-by-side comparison with no animation. The left side shows matching inputs leading to useful outputs. The right side shows mismatched inputs leading to weak or unreliable outputs.

workedExample.scenario: A phone keyboard suggests the next word after someone types: “The meeting starts at 10, please bring the”.
workedExample.input: Text typed so far: “The meeting starts at 10, please bring the”
process: The system reads the sequence of words already typed.
Using patterns learned from training examples, it assigns scores to possible next words such as “report”, “documents”, “files” and “train”.
It ranks the candidates and displays the highest-scoring suggestions.
workedExample.result: The keyboard suggests “report”, “documents” and “files”. It is performing one defined task, predicting likely next words. It does not understand the purpose of the meeting or acquire a broader ability to organise it.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: In a Resident Coordinator's Office, the records officer has until close of business to file the note for the file after a bilateral. The approved records system examines the title and metadata, then recommends one of the office's predefined filing categories.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The classifier may be very accurate at matching records to known categories, but that capability does not extend to judging the substance of the bilateral, drafting follow-up or deciding who should have access. Its competence is narrow and tied to the records task and examples on which it was trained.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: The officer must not upload the note or its contents to an external or unapproved tool. Bilateral records may contain confidential or sensitive information. Only a system approved for the document's classification may process it, and the officer must verify the category and access controls before filing.

whyItMatters: The term helps people ask a basic but important question: what exactly can this system do, and what can it not do? That matters when buying tools, writing policy, setting safeguards, or deciding whether a result needs human review. If people assume a narrow system has broad capability, they may trust it too much, use it on the wrong task, or expose people to avoidable harm. If they recognise its limits, they can match the tool to the job, test it properly, protect sensitive information, and keep accountability with people and organisations rather than with the software.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If a system performs very well on one task, it must be intelligent in a general human-like way.
commonMisconceptions.correction: High performance in one area does not mean broad capability. A system may classify images accurately or generate fluent text while still failing at unrelated tasks, lacking context, or producing errors outside its training and design scope.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Narrow AI only means old, simple systems, not modern chatbots or image tools.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Many modern AI systems are still considered narrow because they operate within particular kinds of tasks and data patterns, even if those tasks are numerous. Being impressive or large does not automatically make a system generally intelligent.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Narrow AI always uses machine learning.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Not always. Some narrow systems are rule-based, meaning they follow explicit instructions written by people. Others use machine learning, where a model is adjusted from examples. Both can be narrow if their scope is limited.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Narrow AI is AI software for specific tasks, rather than broad intellectual work across domains.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Narrow AI refers to systems whose capability is limited to a defined task, domain, or set of related functions. Inputs are processed through rules, statistical models, or learned parameters to produce outputs such as classifications, rankings, predictions, recommendations, or generated content. Performance may be strong within the target distribution, meaning the kinds of examples the system was built or trained for, but it often degrades outside that scope. The term is commonly used in contrast with artificial general intelligence, though the boundary can be blurry for systems that support many related tasks through a shared model.

keyTakeaway: Narrow AI can perform impressively within its defined task and expected inputs, while remaining unreliable or simply incapable outside that scope.

quickCheck.question: Which example best fits narrow AI?
options: A system that can reliably do any intellectual task a person can do
A tool that classifies incoming emails into a few predefined categories
Software that becomes conscious and sets its own goals
A machine that understands the world in the same flexible way humans do
quickCheck.explanation: An AI tool that classifies emails into predefined categories performs a limited, specific task. The other options describe fixed automation, storage software, or broad general capability, not narrow AI.

contested: The general idea is widely used, but the boundary is not fully settled. Newer systems can perform many related tasks, so people may disagree about how narrow they still are and where narrow AI ends and more general capability begins.

issues.problem: The definition is too broad. Any limited-purpose software or automation could satisfy it, even if it is not AI. Its reference to the “full range of human activities” also sets the wrong contrast because general intelligence concerns broad intellectual capability, not every human activity.
issues.fix: An AI system built for a limited task or related tasks, rather than broad intellectual work across domains.

issues.problem: The claim that the system “compares this pattern with many examples seen during training” misstates inference. A trained next-word system normally uses patterns encoded in its trained model. It does not directly compare the current text with many training examples.
issues.fix: It uses patterns learned from many training examples to assess likely next words.

issues.problem: Saying the system is “not understanding every aspect” implies that it may understand some aspects of the meeting. That is unnecessary anthropomorphic framing.
issues.fix: The keyboard suggests 'report', 'documents', and 'files'. This is narrow AI because it performs one defined task: predicting likely next words, not analysing the meeting or performing unrelated tasks.

issues.problem: The visual labels one box as “One narrow AI system” but gives that same system text, image, and number inputs and outputs including translation, spam scoring, next-word prediction, and object detection. Those are different tasks and may require different systems. The diagram therefore blurs the defined scope it is meant to teach.
issues.fix: Use one concrete system throughout. For example, show email text as the expected input, a predefined email category as the useful output, and an image as the out-of-scope input. Make the same change in the accessibility description.

issues.problem: This definition again includes ordinary limited-purpose software and does not distinguish narrow AI from software or automation. “The full range of things a person can do” also includes activities irrelevant to general intelligence.
issues.fix: Narrow AI is AI software for specific tasks, rather than broad intellectual work across domains.

issues.problem: Option 1 is not necessarily AI. A tool can classify emails through fixed rules or ordinary automation, so the marked answer does not establish that the example is narrow AI. The other three options are also implausible near-duplicates about general intelligence or consciousness, making the answer obvious without understanding the distinction.
issues.fix: Replace the options with: ["A fixed script that copies every email into the same folder", "An AI tool that classifies emails into predefined categories", "A database that stores emails but does not classify them", "A general AI that works flexibly across intellectual domains"]

issues.problem: The explanation treats limited classification as sufficient evidence of AI and does not distinguish narrow AI from fixed automation or ordinary software.
issues.fix: An AI tool that classifies emails into predefined categories performs a limited, specific task. The other options describe fixed automation, storage software, or broad general capability, not narrow AI.
